analysis.one_liner: Exempts farmed wetlands from Clean Water Act dredge-and-fill permit requirements.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a single cosponsor, committee vote, or floor vote, and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend the Clean Water Act so that farmers and ranchers could drain, fill, or otherwise alter wetlands on land used for agriculture without first getting a federal permit. The exemption would apply to any wetland farmed in the two years before the law passed, or farmed at least one year since 1972, and would last as long as the land stayed in agricultural production. The bill was sent to the House committee that handles water issues and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Agricultural operators — row-crop farmers, ranchers, timber growers, aquaculture operations, and others covered by the bill's very broad definition of agricultural production — would be freed from the cost, delay, and limits of Clean Water Act Section 404 permits when working farmed wetlands.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would exempt wetlands used for agricultural production from Clean Water Act Section 404 permit requirements for discharges of dredged or fill material [S2][S3].

The exemption would cover any wetland farmed during the twenty-four months before enactment, or farmed at least one year since 1972, and would continue as long as the land remained in agricultural production [S3].

Agricultural production is defined broadly, including row crops, grazing, haying, silviculture (timber), aquaculture and mariculture, livestock raising, water storage and distribution for farming, and construction of farm residences and facilities [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public would bear the cost through the loss of wetlands: fewer federal reviews of ditching, draining, and filling on farmed wetlands, which would allow more conversion of wetlands to fields and pastures, reducing their ability to filter water, store floodwater, and support waterfowl and other wildlife.

drawbacks.text: The exemption would be permanent for as long as land stays in agricultural production, removing ongoing federal review of wetland alterations on millions of farmed acres [S3].

The definition of agricultural production is so broad — including timber, aquaculture, water storage, and farm facility construction — that it could let substantial wetland conversion proceed without the environmental review that a Section 404 permit currently provides [S3].

Farmers already enjoy partial exemptions under Section 404(f) of the Clean Water Act for normal farming activities, so the bill's added benefit would come mainly at the margin, where the environmental risk of unreviewed wetland destruction is greatest [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would save agricultural operators permitting costs and delays, but at the price of removing the main federal check on draining and filling farmed wetlands. Because the exemption would be permanent and the definition of agriculture exceptionally broad, the environmental cost could be large and irreversible, while the farmer benefit is partly redundant with existing exemptions for normal farming. On balance, the bill's main effect is a transfer of regulatory burden from agricultural landholders to the public's wetlands.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Public Works and Transportation Committee and then to its Water Resources Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearings, no votes, and no floor action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Alexander of Arkansas introduced the bill on June 6, 1991 [S1][S5].
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Public Works and Transportation [S5].
On June 20, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources, where no further action is recorded [S5].
No member of the House cosponsored the bill [S4].
The 102nd Congress ended January 3, 1993, with the bill still in subcommittee, so it never received a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Clean Water Act permit requirement for wetland-altering activities on farmed land remained in place, leaving existing wetland protections intact. Agricultural operators did not get the exemption, and the water resources and environmental review status quo was preserved.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no other member signed on, so the bill drew no measurable support or opposition from either party; it died quietly in committee with zero cosponsors [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would exempt farmed wetlands from Clean Water Act Section 404 permitting, saving farm operators the cost and restrictions of federal review when draining or filling wetlands. That gain comes directly at the public's expense in reduced wetland and water-quality protection.

Silviculture is expressly included in the bill's definition of agricultural production, so timber growers on wetland soils would also escape permitting. The public pays in unreviewed wetland conversion.
Aquaculture and mariculture are named in the bill's broad definition of agricultural production, extending the permit exemption to water-based farming. The cost falls on the public's wetlands.

industries.industry: Farm construction and rural development contractors
industries.note: The bill would exempt construction, expansion, and improvement of farm residences and facilities on farmed wetlands from permitting. This lowers builders' costs but permits unreviewed wetland filling.
